spec.focus: Career systems as procedural character generation: how life-sim and strategy games (The Sims, Stardew Valley, Crusader Kings, Dwarf Fortress) design vocational values for recognizability × mechanical legibility × generative combinatorics, and what the 13 proposed values look like when tested against a real procedural generation engine
spec.name: fd-life-sim-career-mechanics
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a life-sim / grand-strategy career-system designer who has shipped or extensively analyzed Sims career tracks, Stardew Valley's occupation-as-relationship-web, Crusader Kings III's character traits-plus-vocation system, or Dwarf Fortress's labor-assignment emergence — they care about whether each vocational value generates distinct observable behaviors, network-relationships, and world-states when run through a procedural engine, measure success by whether the taxonomy produces a combinatorial space that feels richer than the sum of its values, and flag any value that either (a) cannot distinguish itself from adjacent values downstream or (b) over-constrains downstream generation by carrying too many implied traits.
review_areas: The Sims career-track design principle: each career must produce visible, legible status signals that change the character's home, wardrobe, relationship network, and daily schedule in ways a player can recognize without reading a tooltip. Evaluate each of the 13 vocation values against this legibility test: does `trades-transport` produce a truck-driver Unc who looks, sounds, and schedules differently from a `trades-skilled` Unc? If the downstream generator cannot distinguish them visually or behaviorally, the values are effectively collapsed.

Crusader Kings III's character-trait-plus-vocation system teaches a specific lesson about over-specification: when vocation is defined too narrowly (e.g., 'horse-trader' rather than 'merchant'), the combinatorial space collapses because the trait set implied by the vocation leaves no room for interesting variation. Assess whether any of the 13 values are over-specified in this way — does `tech-work` imply so many downstream traits (young, urban, digital-native, ironic) that it over-constrains the generator, effectively producing a single character type rather than a range?

Stardew Valley's design insight: vocation-as-relationship-web matters more than vocation-as-skill-set. The farmer is defined by relationships with seasons, soil, livestock, and market — not by the abstract skill 'farming.' Assess each of the 13 values through this relational lens: what relationships does `land-work` imply (with weather, place, animal, season, market) vs. `service-back-of-house` (with kitchen hierarchy, food supply chains, invisibility, rhythm) — and which values produce the richest relational web for the game's world-building purposes?

Dwarf Fortress's labor emergence principle: when you assign a dwarf a labor, unexpected behaviors cascade from the labor's implied relationships and constraints — miners develop social bonds with other miners, chefs become territorial about kitchens. Evaluate the 13 values for their emergence potential: which vocation values, when combined with the six locked axes, are most likely to produce surprising but coherent Unc characterizations? And which values are too internally homogeneous to generate emergent surprise?

The vocation_formative × vocation_current two-field design creates a trajectory space. From a life-sim mechanics perspective, assess whether the 13 values produce enough interesting trajectory pairs: `military` → `trades-skilled` (the vet who became a contractor) is a well-trodden arc, but `creative-credentialed` → `land-work` (the journalist who bought a farm) is rarer and more characterologically interesting. Does the taxonomy's coverage distribute well across both common and surprising trajectories, or are the common trajectories over-represented?

The `commerce-small` vs `service-customer-facing` boundary is ambiguous from a life-sim mechanics perspective: a long-tenured retail clerk and a small-business owner produce very different economic relationships, asset structures, and social capital — but both 'read people' and both depend on local reputation networks. From a combinatorial-generation standpoint, assess whether this boundary is placed at the right fault line for the game's purposes, or whether the mechanical distinction (owner-operator vs. employee-with-tenure) is load-bearing enough to justify separate values.

severity_examples.condition: If the procedural generator treats both values as 'hands-on physical labor' without additional differentiators, a truck-driver Unc and a carpenter Unc will have overlapping trait sets, similar speech registers, and indistinguishable network-relationships — effectively collapsing two values into one. The life-sim precedent (Sims career tracks) shows this happens when vocation values share too many implied downstream traits.
severity_examples.scenario: `trades-transport` cannot be distinguished from `trades-skilled` in downstream generation

severity_examples.condition: If `tech-work` implies young + urban + ironic + credentialed + high-income in most generation passes, the vocation value is over-constraining the generator — it produces a narrow band of Unc-types (the stereotype) rather than the full range of people who work in tech. A 55-year-old COBOL programmer and a 32-year-old ML engineer are both `tech-work` but should generate very differently, and the taxonomy must allow that range.
severity_examples.scenario: `tech-work` over-specifies downstream traits, collapsing generative range

severity_examples.condition: If the 13 values produce many common trajectory pairs (military → commerce-large, creative-credentialed → creative-freelance) but few surprising ones (service-back-of-house → professional-credentialed, land-work → creative-freelance), the formative × current combinatorics will feel predictable rather than generative. Life-sim design teaches that unexpected trajectories are often the most characterologically interesting ones.
severity_examples.scenario: Trajectory space is skewed toward socially-legible arcs, missing surprising ones

spec.decision_lens: Can a skilled fiction writer generate a fully-realized, non-stereotypical character from this vocation value — or does the value only generate the character's surface, leaving the interior and the metis underdetermined?
spec.focus: Vocation as characterization medium: how working-class realist fiction, hard-boiled crime, and literary journalism characterize people by their work — what makes a vocational type legible on the page, which of the 13 proposed values map to recognizable literary archetypes, and which types of guy the taxonomy leaves unnamed
spec.name: fd-literary-vocation-character
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a literary fiction writer or editor with deep familiarity with working-class realism (Richard Russo, Edward P. Jones, Denis Johnson), hard-boiled crime (Elmore Leonard, George Pelecanos, Laura Lippman), and literary journalism (Tracy Kidder, Adrian Nicole LeBlanc, Mitchell Duneier) — they care about whether each vocation value is capable of generating a fully-realized character who is not reducible to their job, measure success by whether a vocation value produces recognizable speech, body, opinion, and set of attachments, and flag any value that produces a type rather than a person.
review_areas: Richard Russo's `trades-skilled` characters (Mohawk, Nobody's Fool) are defined not by their skill but by their relationship to decline, to pride-without-self-pity, and to the specific geography of deindustrialized small-city life. Assess whether the proposed value carries these characterological implications or only the surface attribute (hands, tools, problem-solving). A vocation value that only generates surface attributes will produce flat characters in the downstream Unc generator — the metis must include the emotional and social texture, not just the technical.

Denis Johnson's `service-back-of-house` characters (Jesus' Son, Tree of Smoke) reveal that kitchen and service labor produces a specific relationship to time, to invisibility, and to professional competence that exists entirely outside credentialed recognition. Assess whether `service-back-of-house` is sufficiently distinct from `service-customer-facing` to generate this interior — or whether the split between back and front of house is doing less characterological work than it appears (both produce people who are institutionally competent but institutionally invisible).

Elmore Leonard's characters are almost entirely vocation-defined — his criminals, detectives, lawyers, and repo men are their work in a way that produces specific speech registers, specific attachments, and specific forms of dignity. Evaluate the 13 values against the Leonard criterion: does each value produce a distinctive speech register (not just vocabulary, but rhythm, indirection, and the specific things a person of this vocation treats as too obvious to say)? Values that produce indistinct speech registers are characterologically under-specified.

Adrian Nicole LeBlanc's `caregiver` characters in 'Random Family' reveal that social work, care work, and domestic management exist in a metis-space that is entirely illegible to credentialed systems — but they are not a single type. Assess the `caregiver` bundling specifically: the EMT's metis (triage, physical management of crisis) produces a different character than the hospice worker's metis (waiting, presence, the long goodbye) or the parish priest's metis (ritual, community memory, moral authority). Does the value's coarsening produce a character who cannot be distinguished from any of these — and is that an acceptable loss for the game's purposes?

Mitchell Duneier's `commerce-small` characters (sidewalk vendors, bookstore owners) carry a specific set of attachments: to place, to regular customers, to the microeconomy of reputation. Assess whether `commerce-small` adequately captures the distinction between the independent-contractor-with-reputation (whose capital is skill-and-word-of-mouth) and the shopkeeper (whose capital is place-and-regular-customers). These produce different Uncs — the contractor is itinerant and portable, the shopkeeper is rooted and vulnerable to displacement. Does the taxonomy need a modifier or does the class-coding + region-coding cross-product handle this?

The underground-economy gap (the brief explicitly names 'numbers runner, weed dealer pre-legalization, bootlegger' as potential missing types): literary fiction has a rich vocabulary for this type (Donald Goines, Chester Himes, The Wire) but the current taxonomy has no home for it. Assess what vocation value the informal-economy worker would fall under and whether the absence is a gap or an intentional exclusion. The brief names it as a question — this agent should give a concrete answer.

severity_examples.condition: The numbers runner, the unlicensed contractor, the pre-legalization weed dealer, and the grey-market fixer are recognizable and culturally distinct types of guy that the current taxonomy cannot express. If the game's procedural generator cannot produce these types, it has a coverage gap that will be noticed by players who recognize them from fiction (The Wire, Donald Goines, Elmore Leonard) and wonder why they don't appear.
severity_examples.scenario: No vocation value can generate informal/underground-economy Uncs

severity_examples.condition: If the downstream characterization system cannot distinguish the EMT's crisis-triage interior from the hospice worker's long-patience interior from the priest's community-ritual interior, the value is generating a type ('caring person') rather than a character. Literary fiction's test: a skilled writer given only the value `caregiver` cannot write a fully-realized Unc without additional disambiguation — they need to know which kind of caregiver.
severity_examples.scenario: `caregiver` produces a single interior regardless of specific care-work type

severity_examples.condition: If `professional-credentialed` produces Uncs whose distinguishing characteristic is status and credential rather than the specific metis of their practice (the lawyer's knowledge of what language can and cannot do; the dentist's knowledge of what people hide in their mouths; the engineer's knowledge of failure modes), the value generates surface without interior. The Leonard criterion: what does a `professional-credentialed` Unc treat as too obvious to say?
severity_examples.scenario: `professional-credentialed` generates flat high-status characters without metis texture

success_hints: The Leonard test for each value: what does a character of this vocation treat as too obvious to say? What is the thing they know that they assume everyone knows, but don't? Values that cannot answer this question are generating surface, not interior.

The LeBlanc test for `caregiver`: can a skilled writer distinguish the five subtypes within the value from the value label alone, or does disambiguation require additional information? If the latter, the value needs either a split or a sub-type modifier.

Check each value against the 'non-stereotypical character' criterion: can the value generate a character who confounds the stereotype of that vocation while remaining recognizably of that type? Values that only generate the stereotype have no room for the Uncanny signature (the thing he loves that doesn't fit his type).

spec.decision_lens: How does this density option behave when the player's actual walk is 800m, or 12 minutes, or interrupted, or driven in a car — and which option is most robust to the full variance of real GPS sessions?
spec.focus: Real-world density curves: GPS session shapes, walk-length distributions, time-of-day effects, weather dropout, and how density options interact with actual human movement patterns
spec.name: fd-location-game-ops
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a walking/location-game ops specialist with hands-on experience from Pokémon GO, Ingress, and Wizards Unite — they care about how density options perform against real GPS session shapes (not idealized walks), measure success by whether the density curve produces satisfying encounters across the full range of player movement contexts (lunch walks, dog walks, commutes, hikes), and flag any density option that works in the design doc but breaks against real-world GPS noise, short sessions, and non-linear routes.
review_areas: Real Pokémon GO session data shows a bimodal walk-length distribution: most sessions are under 1km (lunch, dog walk, errand) with a secondary peak at 3–5km (dedicated walk). Option C's ~1 per km cap of 3–4 makes it generous for dedicated walkers but produces only 0–1 encounters for the majority short-session players — assess whether Option C is inadvertently a 'dedicated walker' design that underserves casual sessions.

Option B's wildcard trigger at >2km / >30min is a hard cliff — players who walk 1.9km get nothing extra, players who walk 2.1km get a chance at a second Unc. Assess whether this cliff creates a 'just one more block' optimization loop that conflicts with the slow-game aesthetic, and whether a softer gradient (probability increases continuously with distance) would serve the design better.

GPS drift in urban environments (building canyons, tree cover, subway exits) produces phantom movement of 20–200m — at Option C density, this could trigger spurious encounter eligibility in players who are standing still. Evaluate whether the distance-gated options need a minimum speed filter and how that filter interacts with the slow-walker population (elderly players, parents with strollers).

The brief mentions 'time-gated rather than distance-gated' as an unexplored alternative. Evaluate this against the four options: a time-gated design (one Unc per session regardless of distance) is GPS-noise-immune and equalizes sessions across mobility levels, but may over-reward car rides. Assess whether Unc Rancher's lure mechanic already implies a time gate (lure ends when player ends walk) and whether Option A is already de facto time-gated.

Weather and seasonal effects on walk frequency are significant in location games — Pokémon GO saw 30–40% session drops in winter and rain. Assess whether any density option creates a 'weather trap' where players who walk in bad conditions get worse outcomes (Option D's probability gating could disadvantage short winter walks if lure quality correlates with walk investment).

The 'asynchronous Unc' alternative (Uncs appear at routes walked before, ambient) is a fundamentally different session shape — it rewards route familiarity rather than active walking, and creates a pull back to known geography. Evaluate this against real-world location-game retention data: Ingress's portal-revisit mechanic drove consistent daily routing, which may or may not fit the slow-game ethos.

severity_examples.condition: If >60% of real sessions are under 1km (consistent with Pokémon GO session data), Option C produces 0–1 encounters for most players most of the time — functionally equivalent to Option A but without the guaranteed-satisfaction contract, yielding the worst of both worlds.
severity_examples.scenario: Option C under-delivers on short sessions that represent majority of plays

severity_examples.condition: In dense urban environments, GPS drift of 50–150m is common for a stationary phone. Under Option C, a player standing outside a building could accumulate enough 'distance' for 1–2 encounters without walking — this is a detectable exploit but also a false-positive that trains the wrong session behavior.
severity_examples.scenario: GPS drift triggers encounter eligibility for stationary players

severity_examples.condition: Players who learn the 2km wildcard threshold will extend walks specifically to hit it, shifting the session goal from 'walk with the lure' to 'walk to the threshold' — this is a subtle but detectable shift from vibe-driven to optimization-driven play.
severity_examples.scenario: Option B's 2km cliff creates walk-length optimization pressure

success_hints: Map each density option against three canonical session archetypes: the 800m lunch walk, the 3km weekend walk, and the interrupted 20-minute walk with GPS dropout. A density design should satisfy at least two of the three without requiring the player to optimize.

The time-gated alternative (one Unc per completed session) is GPS-noise-immune and mobility-equitable — it deserves explicit evaluation as a v0 simplification before distance-gating complexity is committed.
Check whether Option A is already de facto time-gated given the lure mechanic: if one lure = one walk = one Unc, the effective gate is player intent (starting a lure walk) not distance covered.
spec.task_context: Reviewing the four encounter density options (A/B/C/D) for Unc Rancher v0 through a location-game operations lens — assessing how each option performs against real-world GPS session shapes, mobility variance, and failure modes that only appear when players walk actual streets.

spec.decision_lens: Does the formula's compositional shape produce the right routing behavior at the edges of its parameter space (sun_coefficient=0, sun_fraction=0, sun_fraction=1, very long edges, very short non-degenerate edges)? Is the un-routable case categorically separated from the multiplicative cost, or could a future loss term be tempted to encode blockage as a large multiplier? Is the formula dimensionally consistent in a way Phase 2's UTCI weight will be able to follow?
spec.distance_rationale: Open-channel hydraulics with per-reach loss coefficients and sluice-gate blocking is centuries and disciplines removed from Python Protocol design for graph routing, yet shares the deep structure of composing a traversal cost from a length term and a multiplicative impedance term with un-traversable cases.
spec.expected_isomorphisms: A millwright costs a head of water as length-times-slope minus per-reach loss (debris, weed, masonry roughness) and treats a closed sluice not as a 'very lossy reach' but as a categorically un-traversable element — the wheel does not turn at all. Mapped: felt-minutes = (length/pace) × (1 + k × sun_fraction) is a length-times-impedance composition; +inf for degenerate_zero_length is the closed-sluice case. The millwright tradition's hard-won lesson is that lumping the closed-sluice case into the loss-coefficient family (very high k) is what produces phantom water — exactly the 'free teleport' failure mode the brainstorm names. The framework asks whether the composition law is honestly separated from the blockage law, and whether the per-reach loss term is dimensionally and monotonically sane.
spec.focus: Whether the multiplicative composition `(walking_minutes) × (1 + sun_coefficient × sun_fraction)` is the right shape, whether the +inf branch is properly walled off from the multiplicative branch, and whether the formula admits the dimensional/monotonicity checks a centuries-old craft would demand of any per-segment cost.
spec.name: fd-mill-race-composition
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a master millwright tracing the head loss down a mill race reach by reach — for whom a per-reach cost must be dimensionally honest, monotonic in the obvious direction, and categorically distinct from a closure. The framework treats the felt-minute formula as a head-loss equation and asks whether its multiplicative structure has the right invariants under the operations Phase 1.7 will perform on it (sum along a path, compare across paths, scale by pace).
review_areas: Multiplicative-vs-additive shape: `time × (1 + k×sf)` makes the sun penalty proportional to walking time, which is defensible (more sun-exposure for longer walks), but is this stated as a design intent or assumed? Additive `time + k×sf×length` is the obvious alternative and gives qualitatively different routing on long-vs-short edges

Monotonicity guarantee under composition: the unit test asserts monotonicity in sun_fraction for fixed length, but A* sums felt-minutes along paths — is the sum monotonic in the obvious way (a route with one extra fully-sunny edge is never preferred over the same route without it, all else equal)? The brainstorm does not state this path-level invariant

+inf wall-off: degenerate_zero_length returns +inf BEFORE the multiplicative branch — good. But the Protocol contract says 'returns +inf for un-routable edges (degenerate zero-length, missing required attrs)' yet `FeltMinutesV0` only emits +inf for the zero-length case; missing `length` defaults to 0.0 which produces 0.0 felt-minutes, NOT +inf. This is the closed-sluice-as-zero-loss failure mode

Dimensional consistency: `walking_minutes` has units of minutes; `(1 + k × sun_fraction)` is dimensionless; product is minutes — clean. But `sun_coefficient = 0.5` is a pure number with no documented meaning (is it dimensionless? per-fraction? per-fraction-per-minute?). Phase 2's UTCI will need to extend this and a unit-free coefficient invites confusion

Coefficient-zero and coefficient-large limits: at `sun_coefficient=0` the formula degenerates to pure walking time (good — matches dawn/dusk reasoning). At very large `sun_coefficient` (e.g., 10) a fully-sunny short edge can outweigh a fully-shaded long edge — is there a documented sensible upper bound for tuning, or is the parameter space silently unbounded?

Composition with future weights: the brainstorm says Phase 2 UTCI / checkpoint / elevation will implement the same Protocol independently. But how do two EdgeWeight implementations combine in Phase 2 (sum? max? weighted blend?)? The Protocol shape forecloses this — there is no combinator. A millwright would ask: how do I sum head losses across reaches when two losses act on the same reach?

spec.name: fd-mobile-airquality-calibration
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a mobile air quality monitoring scientist who designs route-based sensor campaigns, validates modeled concentration maps against fixed reference stations, and quantifies how sensor bias propagates into exposure assessments.
review_areas: The shadow raster is the output of a ray-tracing model (build_shadow.py) over a LIDAR DSM — it has never been validated against field observations (photos, shadow meter, GPS-tagged shade walks). Mobile monitoring practice requires at least a spot-check co-location before operational use; the brainstorm deploys the raster into routing without any validation step

The Phase 1.3 measurement of '12.4% shade at 3pm summer' is used as a sanity check (mean sun_fraction should be 0.6–0.95) but this is circular validation — if build_shadow.py has a systematic error (e.g., DSM height offset, sun-vector azimuth error), both the raster and the acceptance criterion would be wrong in the same direction

The routing weight formula time × (1 + 0.5 × sun_fraction) treats sun_fraction as a calibrated physical quantity, but the raster encodes a binary instantaneous state at a single timestamp — mobile monitoring practice requires assessing temporal representativeness before using a single-pass measurement to characterize a route

The CRS assertion (EPSG:32611) is the only data-quality gate in the brainstorm. Mobile monitoring practice would also verify raster date/time against solar geometry to confirm the sun vector used in build_shadow.py matches actual solar position at the timestamp claimed in the filename

The sun_timestamp attribute carries the timestamp forward to Phase 1.6 but there is no validation that the timestamp in the filename matches the EXIF/metadata timestamp inside the GeoTIFF — a file rename or copy could silently decouple the two

If the DSM has vertical errors (common in urban canyon LIDAR where reflections off glass cause false height spikes), some building shadows will be systematically too long or too short. The brainstorm has no mechanism to flag edges where sun_fraction disagrees with a reference (e.g., known open plazas that should be >95% sun)

severity_examples.example: The shadow raster timestamp is parsed from the filename only — there is no check that the filename timestamp matches the GeoTIFF's internal metadata or the solar geometry parameters used by build_shadow.py. A raster regenerated with a corrected sun vector but saved over the old filename would produce wrong sun_fraction values attributed to the correct timestamp, propagating silently through all downstream routing.

The 12.4% shade measurement from Phase 1.3 is used as the acceptance criterion baseline ('mean sun_fraction should be 0.6–0.95') but this is the model's own output, not a ground-truth observation. If build_shadow.py's sun-vector or DSM is systematically wrong, the raster and the acceptance test would both be wrong in the same direction, and the smoke test would pass while routing weights are meaningfully miscalibrated.

The brainstorm does not specify what a 'believable distribution' means beyond the range check. Mobile monitoring practice would require a reference segment — one known-sunny block and one known-shady block — with expected sun_fraction bounds as regression anchors. Without these, raster quality degrades silently across iterations of build_shadow.py.

spec.name: fd-mobile-retention-lifecycle
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a mobile-game retention analyst with experience reading cohort curves for walking and collection games — they care about which density option produces the most durable engagement curve without a metrics treadmill, measure success by whether the game's D30 retention is driven by intrinsic walk motivation rather than fear of missing encounters, and flag any density option whose short-term engagement pattern produces a long-term churn cliff.
review_areas: Empty-walk churn risk (Options A/D): location games that produce empty sessions — walks where the player gets no Unc — risk training players that the game is unreliable. Analyze the Option D probability distribution: a 50% common-lure encounter rate means that a new player doing 3 walks in their first week has a 12.5% chance of getting nothing across all three sessions, a first-week churn risk that is unusually high for an onboarding period.

Over-frequency churn risk (Option C): retention analysis of Pokémon GO shows that engagement spikes at launch then drops sharply when the 'collection complete' feeling arrives. Option C's 3–4 encounters per walk at 5km means a dedicated walker accumulates 20–25 Uncs per week — assess the implied 'felt-complete' timeline and whether the game's Unc variety space can sustain that pace.

Lure-reuse behavior shapes long-term density differently than first-session density — a player who has 50 songs/films in their media library will cycle lures more slowly than a player who only uses their current favorite album. Assess whether any density option creates a 'lure treadmill' pressure (needing to consume new media to unlock new Unc families) that conflicts with the game's no-microtransaction/no-spam ethos.

The 'reversibility' criterion from the brief — which option is hardest to reverse? — has a specific retention implication: if players build habits around Option A's 'guaranteed one per walk' promise and the team later shifts to Option C, existing players experience a density reduction as a loss even if new players find it generous. Assess which option creates the most durable commitment at the habit level.

D7 retention in walking games is strongly predicted by whether players return for a second and third walk in the first week. Assess which density option best supports a first-week habit formation loop: Option A's guaranteed satisfaction may be optimal for D7 even if it is less engaging at D30; Option D's probabilistic structure may produce higher D30 among players who survive D7 but higher D7 churn among players who don't.

The 'no notification spam' design principle (from the brief) constrains re-engagement mechanics — the game cannot pull players back with push notifications about waiting Uncs. Assess whether any density option creates a natural re-engagement trigger that does not require notifications (e.g., Option B's wildcard creating 'I wonder if the walk was long enough' anticipation, or Option D's lure-quality system creating 'I have a good lure saved' holding behavior).

severity_examples.condition: A new player who walks three times in their first week with common lures has a 12.5% chance of three empty sessions — this is a quantifiable onboarding failure rate that will manifest as visible D7 churn for a significant cohort. Without a consolation mechanism (a 'near miss' signal, a lore reason for failure), these players attribute failure to the app rather than to the design.
severity_examples.scenario: Option D first-week triple empty-walk churn cliff

severity_examples.condition: If v0 ships with N Unc families and Option C produces 20–25 encounters per week for dedicated walkers, the expected time to 'I've seen everything' is N/20 weeks — if that number is under 8 weeks, the game needs either a content update schedule or a density reduction to sustain D60+ retention, and content updates at that cadence are a v0 cost commitment the brief explicitly wants to minimize.
severity_examples.scenario: Option C 'felt-complete' arc too short for v0 Unc variety space

severity_examples.condition: If encounter outcomes are strongly tied to lure novelty (new lures = new Unc families, repeated lures = same Unc families), players who exhaust their media library face implicit pressure to consume new media to unlock new encounters — this is a soft microtransaction substitute that conflicts with the no-treadmill design principle.
severity_examples.scenario: Lure-reuse pressure creates implicit consumption treadmill

success_hints: Model three player archetypes: the casual walker (3 walks/week, 1km average), the regular walker (5 walks/week, 3km average), and the dedicated walker (daily, 5km+). Each density option should produce a satisfying 6-month curve for at least two of the three archetypes without optimization pressure.

The no-notification constraint is a design forcing function — the game's re-engagement loop must be intrinsic. Identify whether each density option creates a natural 'reason to return' that does not rely on push mechanics (anticipation, held lures, route familiarity).

Option A's reversibility risk: if guaranteed-one-per-walk becomes the player's mental contract with the game, downgrading to Option C later is perceived as a nerf even if the average encounters-per-week is the same. Flag this as a commitment the team makes at launch.

spec.decision_lens: The recommendation system designer asks: (1) Does the bias-roll matrix produce sufficient intra-type diversity — two Uncs with the same politics value but different class/region/era combinations should feel meaningfully different, not like the same character with different metadata? spec.distance_rationale: Orthogonal — music recommendation system design is a professional engineering discipline for encoding correlated multi-axis typed generators that produce varied-but-coherent outputs from a seed, operating at the same abstraction level as the bias-roll matrix (a conditional-probability table for correlated typed generation) but for a completely different purpose (music playlist generation for listener engagement, not procedural character generation for a walking app).
spec.expected_isomorphisms: The music recommendation discipline's 'genre lock' problem (a strong axis seed overrides all other axes, eliminating diversity) maps directly to the bias-roll matrix's risk that the Ghitza-Gelman cohort-imprinting multipliers are strong enough to produce near-deterministic outputs for specific axis combinations — both domains resolved this by specifying maximum multiplier magnitudes. spec.focus: Music recommendation and playlist generation system design — how practitioners encode multi-axis taste graphs (genre, era, tempo, mood, instrumentation, cultural origin) as correlated typed generators where a user seed in one axis probabilistically surfaces content along multiple correlated axes, what the craft of taste-graph stratified sampling reveals about the brainstorm's app-scoped code-location decision and schema evolution, and how the playlist-generation discipline handles the 'adjacent-but-different' recommendation problem that maps to the Unc diversity requirement
spec.name: fd-music-rec-taste-graph-axis-encoding
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a senior music recommendation system designer with experience building taste-graph engines (think: Spotify's audio features + genre taxonomy, Pandora's Music Genome Project axis encoding). They care about whether a multi-axis correlated generator produces variety within a type (two `true-believer` Uncs should feel different from each other even if their politics value is the same), whether the schema is evolvable as new axis values are added (Pandora adds new genome axes without retraining the full correlation model), and whether the app-scoped code location creates a schema-evolution bottleneck when axes are added or recalibrated. They measure success by whether the generated outputs feel like a playlist — coherent as a set, varied within the set, non-repetitive across a session.
review_areas: Intra-type diversity and the variety-within-coherence requirement: Pandora's Music Genome Project learned that a taste axis system that maximizes inter-type distinctiveness (different genres sound very different) at the expense of intra-type variety (all songs in one genre sound the same) produces listener fatigue. The bias-roll matrix must allow two Uncs with the same `politics-posture` to feel meaningfully different — driven by their class, region, and era. Review whether the 9 bias families, as described, produce sufficient within-value diversity, or whether the biases are so strong that a given politics value produces a nearly deterministic combination of other axis values.

Schema evolution bottleneck and the app-scoped location decision: decision 2 in the brainstorm places the matrix at `apps/uncrancher/data/bias-roll.yaml`. Spotify's recommendation architecture separates the axis taxonomy schema (shared across teams) from the content-axis feature extraction (app-scoped) from the taste-graph correlation model (separately versioned). Review whether placing the bias-roll matrix entirely within the uncrancher app creates a schema-evolution bottleneck when new axes are added to the Unc ontology (e.g., if a future bead adds a 'religiosity' axis, who owns the update to the bias-roll matrix?) and whether the Zod schema's validation approach is compatible with schema evolution without breaking existing YAML entries.

Adjacent-but-different generation and the hard-boundary problem: recommendation systems discovered that hard boundaries between cell values (genre = jazz vs genre = blues) produce unnatural discontinuities where slightly different seeds produce radically different outputs. Pandora's solution was continuous latent-space representations; simpler systems use soft-boundary multipliers (a jazz-coded track gets a non-zero but depressed weight in blues recommendations). Review whether the YAML conditional-rule format, which uses discrete axis values in `when:` clauses, can express soft-boundary effects — or whether a `working-class × Rust Belt × Vietnam-era` Unc that should feel adjacent to a `working-class × Appalachian × Vietnam-era` Unc will instead feel discontinuously different because the conditional rules fire separately for each region value.

Session-level diversity and the re-lure cooldown interaction: the brainstorm explicitly defers 're-lure cooldown logic (24h same-lure → common-tier-only rolls)' to v1+. Recommendation systems have learned that session-level diversity requires state management — the same playlist algorithm run twice on the same seed produces the same output without session-state injection. Review whether the bias-roll matrix's design (stateless conditional rules applied to each roll independently) is compatible with the eventual v1+ cooldown requirement, or whether supporting cooldown will require a structural change to how the matrix is applied.

Axis addition and backward compatibility: Pandora's Music Genome Project was designed with explicit backward compatibility for axis addition — new genome axes can be added without invalidating existing axis-correlation data. Review whether the brainstorm's Zod schema handles axis addition gracefully (does the schema allow unknown axis keys in `when:` clauses for forward compatibility, or does it reject them with a validation error?) and whether the Option ε schema reservation (`deviationRollFor`, `expectedFlavor` fields) follows the same backward-compatibility discipline.

The stub compatibility contract and the playlist-as-session framing: decision 9 in the brainstorm specifies that `rollStubUnc({walkId, lure})` signature is preserved. In recommendation-system terms, this is the seed-to-playlist API — the same seed should produce the same playlist (deterministic given the seed), but a walk-level session should produce a varied set of Uncs across multiple rolls. Review whether the matrix's deterministic seeding (via `walkId` and `lure.id`) is compatible with the session-variety requirement — specifically, whether two rolls with the same walkId but different lure.ids will produce appropriately varied Uncs or whether the bias matrix's strongest cells will dominate both rolls.

severity_examples.condition: The brainstorm does not specify maximum multiplier magnitudes for any bias family. Recommendation-system practice caps individual axis-weight contributions to preserve diversity; without explicit caps, the strongest empirically-grounded cells will dominate the matrix and undermine the Unc variety requirement.
severity_examples.scenario: If the Ghitza-Gelman cohort-imprinting bias family applies a very strong multiplier (e.g., 5×-10×) to `working-class × Appalachian × Vietnam-era → traditionally-loyal`, the effective probability for that cell becomes so dominant that the bias-roll matrix produces nearly deterministic outputs for that combination — two Uncs from that cell will differ only in the weaker downstream axes. In recommendation-system terms, this is the 'genre lock' problem: a strong enough genre seed overrides all other axes, producing outputs that feel like the same track played repeatedly.

severity_examples.condition: If the Zod schema strictly validates axis names and rejects unknown values, adding a new axis requires a two-step coordinated deploy (schema update + YAML update), which is a schema-evolution bottleneck. Recommendation-system architecture would make this a one-step operation by allowing unknown axis values to default to neutral multipliers.
severity_examples.scenario: The app-scoped location decision (`apps/uncrancher/data/bias-roll.yaml`) means that adding a new axis to the Unc ontology requires a coordinated update to the bias-roll YAML, the Zod schema, and the roll engine. In recommendation systems, this is the 'cold-start' problem for new features — a new axis has no correlation data, so the matrix must assign it a neutral multiplier (1.0) until data is available. The brainstorm does not specify how new axes are handled in the Zod schema (does the schema fail if a `when:` clause references an unknown axis, or does it default to neutral?).

severity_examples.condition: Recommendation systems handle this with slot-indexed seeds (`hash(userId, sessionId, slotIndex)`). The brainstorm's stub-compat contract preserves the `rollStubUnc({walkId, lure})` signature but does not address multi-Unc-per-lure generation — the roll engine (solwend-1zp) will need to add a slot parameter when that feature arrives.
severity_examples.scenario: The brainstorm's deterministic seeding (via `walkId` and `lure.id`) means that the same walk will always produce the same Unc for the same lure, which is the correct behavior for the replay/consistency requirement. But if multiple Uncs are generated per walk (e.g., the porch has multiple Uncs visible simultaneously), the seeding scheme must produce distinct results for each Unc slot while remaining deterministic. If the seed is simply `hash(walkId, lure.id)` without a slot index, all Unc slots for the same lure will produce the same Unc.

review_areas: The formula computes (length_m / self.pace_mps) / 60.0 — if pace_mps = 0.0 (a misconfigured instance), this produces ZeroDivisionError in Python (not IEEE 754 inf, because Python float division by zero raises). The brainstorm specifies frozen=True prevents mutation after construction but no validation on __post_init__ prevents FeltMinutesV0(pace_mps=0.0) — the error surfaces at runtime during A*, not at construction time, making it hard to trace.

The contract states 'Never NaN, never negative — these break Dijkstra/A* preconditions.' The NaN fallback dispatch branches on math.isnan(sf) where sf comes from edge_attrs.get('sun_fraction', ???). The brainstorm's pseudocode uses edge_attrs.get('sun_fraction', 0.0) as the default — if the key is absent and the fallback is 0.0, the NaN policy is never invoked, and the edge is treated as fully shaded (multiplier = 1.0) rather than unknown — the brainstorm should document whether absent sun_fraction should trigger the NaN fallback or default to shaded.

For NaN fallback policy 'constant', _effective_sun_fraction returns nan_fallback_value (default 0.5). If a caller passes FeltMinutesV0(nan_fallback_value=float('nan')), the NaN fallback produces NaN — a NaN that bypasses the isnan check because it is not from the edge attribute, violating the contract. The brainstorm does not guard nan_fallback_value against NaN.

sun_coefficient * effective_sun_fraction where both are valid floats in [0,1] is safe — but the brainstorm uses 1.0 + sun_coefficient * sf without bounding sun_coefficient. A caller passing sun_coefficient=-1.0 produces a multiplier of 1 + (-1)(0.5) = 0.5, resulting in felt_minutes < walking_minutes — a weight that rewards sun exposure, inverting the formula. No guard is specified.

The brainstorm's smoke test asserts 'felt_minutes == inf for degenerate_zero_length edges' using == comparison — math.inf == math.inf is True in Python (unlike NaN), so this is numerically correct. However, the smoke test also checks 'wall-clock < 2s on the 12,880-edge DTLA graph' — this is not a deterministic assertion (depends on machine load) and the brainstorm does not specify what to do if the smoke test fails this timing constraint in CI.

spec.name: fd-numerical-sampling-correctness
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a numerical computing engineer who reviews vectorized pipelines for silent precision and counting errors — they care about whether sample counts, NaN masking, and integer pixel indexing produce the claimed result, measure correctness by checking boundary conditions (zero-length edge, single-sample edge, all-nodata block), and flag anywhere that Python int() truncation, np.linspace endpoint semantics, or boolean sum casting could introduce systematic bias.
review_areas: The sample count formula `n = max(2, int(np.ceil(geom.length / interval_m)) + 1)` — the `+1` makes this a fence-post count (N intervals → N+1 points), which combined with `np.linspace(0.0, geom.length, n)` is correct, but the brainstorm's decision table says 'min 2 samples per edge' while the formula gives n=2 only when geom.length < interval_m; a zero-length degenerate edge (length=0.0) gives ceil(0/5)+1=1, hitting max(2,...) = 2 samples both at t=0.0, which are the same point — the brainstorm should acknowledge this.

The pseudocode computes `in_sun = int((vals == 0).sum())` and `in_shade = int((vals == 1).sum())` as Python ints; if vals is a uint8 numpy array with ~40k entries, `.sum()` on a boolean array returns numpy.int64 which is fine, but casting to Python int before division `in_sun / total` yields Python float — this is correct but the brainstorm does not document the type pathway, leaving risk of someone replacing with `//` or numpy integer division.

The `cols, rows = inv * (pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])` step produces float pixel coordinates; `rows.astype(int)` uses numpy's default truncation (floor for positive, ceiling for negative) rather than nearest-neighbor rounding — for a pixel center at 0.5, a sample at exactly that world coordinate rounds down to pixel 0 rather than the nearest pixel, introducing a systematic half-pixel bias at building edges.

The nodata exclusion `total = in_sun + in_shade` (where nodata pixels contribute 0 to both) is correct, but if `vals` contains values other than 0, 1, and 255 (e.g., due to a corrupt raster or wrong band), those values are silently dropped from total without warning — the brainstorm should specify whether unknown values are treated as nodata or trigger an error.

The vectorized `pts` array is built as `np.array([geom.interpolate(t).coords[0] for t in ts])` — this is a Python list comprehension, not vectorized; for edges with many samples (a 200m boulevard at 5m interval = 41 samples) this is acceptable, but the brainstorm claims 'vectorized NumPy raster lookup' which is only true for the pixel-lookup step, not the point-generation step; this distinction matters for the < 5s performance claim.

severity_examples.condition: If the OSM graph contains collapsed edges (length=0.0 from node deduplication), both samples land at the same pixel — this is a tautological measurement, not representative of the edge. If that pixel happens to be nodata, the edge gets NaN; if it's shade, sun_fraction=0.0. The brainstorm does not flag this as a known artifact.
severity_examples.scenario: Zero-length degenerate edge gets 2 identical samples

severity_examples.condition: Systematic floor truncation means samples just inside a shaded building footprint round to the sun pixel, biasing sun_fraction upward by up to one pixel width (1m) at every building edge. For short edges (8m alley, 2 samples) this can flip the majority vote.
severity_examples.scenario: Truncation vs rounding at pixel boundaries

severity_examples.condition: A raster with a third value (e.g., 128 for 'partial shade' added by a future build_shadow version) would be silently excluded from total, making sun_fraction look higher than it is with no warning.
severity_examples.scenario: Silent drop of unexpected raster values

success_hints: Document the degenerate edge behavior (length=0, or length < interval_m) explicitly and specify whether it is treated as a warning or is acceptable given short-edge rarity.
Use `np.round(cols).astype(int)` rather than `.astype(int)` for pixel coordinate conversion to avoid systematic half-pixel bias.
Add a validation step that checks `np.any((vals != 0) & (vals != 1) & (vals != nodata))` and logs a warning if unexpected values appear.
spec.task_context: Reviewing the brainstorm's numerical sampling design for arithmetic correctness, boundary conditions, and silent bias sources that would affect sun_fraction accuracy.

Do not address the broader game design, encounter mechanics, or lure design — focus only on whether the proposed vocation values cluster occupations whose demand profiles produce coherent and distinguishable embodied identities
spec.decision_lens: The OT asks: which of the 13 proposed values cluster occupations with incoherent demand profiles — different postures, different attention rhythms, different social-load signatures? If a vocation value groups someone whose primary demand is sustained fine-motor precision with someone whose primary demand is gross-motor strength and weather-exposure, the taxonomy is grouping bodies that will not look, move, or age the same way.
spec.distance_rationale: Orthogonal — occupational therapy and vocational rehabilitation is a licensed professional discipline that classifies occupations by functional demand profile for clinical and return-to-work purposes. It operates at the same abstraction level as our taxonomy (grouping kinds-of-work by shared characteristics) but uses a completely different clustering criterion (what the job does to a person's body and attention over years of practice). This is the closest professional analog to the brief's own stated concern: vocation produces bodies, gait, hands, posture.
expected_isomorphisms: OT physical demand profile coherence ↔ vocation value body-formation coherence: the brief states that different vocations produce different walks and that vocation is durably embodied even in retirement — the OT demand-profile test directly validates whether each proposed value will produce a distinctive and recognizable embodied Unc

DOT/O*NET attention-rhythm categories ↔ character personality-facet downstream distributions: burst-peak attention rhythm (surgeon, musician) vs. sustained monotonic attention (driver, data-entry) vs. ambient social-scanning (bartender, teacher) will produce different personality-facet distributions in the generation system — the OT can predict which values need to be split to avoid incoherent downstream distributions

Vocational rehabilitation's `functional capacity residue` concept ↔ `vocation_formative` × `way-depth = lifer` mechanic: the OT discipline has formalized the idea that past vocational demands leave durable functional traces in the body — this is the clearest professional analog to the brief's Berlant/Scott substrates for why `vocation_formative` must be a separate field
spec.focus: Occupational therapy and work-demand analysis — how OT practitioners classify occupations by physical, cognitive, social, and temporal demand profiles for return-to-work and vocational rehabilitation, what those demand profiles reveal about body-formation and identity, and where the proposed 13 values cluster occupations with incoherent demand profiles
spec.name: fd-occupational-therapy-work-demand-profile
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a certified occupational therapist specializing in vocational rehabilitation and functional capacity evaluation — they care about what a job actually does to a person's body and cognition over years of practice, how different demand profiles produce different physical signatures (posture, hand strength, pain patterns, attention rhythms), and how the functional-demand profile of a vocation becomes identity-constitutive in ways that persist into retirement and disability.
review_areas: Physical demand coherence of `trades-skilled`: the Dictionary of Occupational Titles (DOT) and its successor O*NET classify trades by physical demand level (sedentary / light / medium / heavy / very heavy) and primary exertion type. Electricians (climbing, reaching, fine-motor wiring) and masons (heavy lifting, sustained kneeling, material handling) have different DOT physical demand profiles despite sharing a `trades-skilled` label. The bodies these vocations produce over 30 years are different.

`caregiver` demand-profile incoherence: the OT discipline splits caregiving occupations sharply by demand profile — direct patient-handling (nurse, home health aide, EMT — high physical demand, musculoskeletal injury risk, fatigue patterns) vs. relationship-sustained service (K-12 teacher, social worker, librarian — low physical demand, high sustained-attention demand, emotional-labor profile). These produce different bodies and different psychological signature.

Cognitive demand and attention rhythm as identity-formation: the OT O*NET data distinguishes occupations by sustained attention duration, divided attention, near-vision demand, and information-processing load. The `creative-freelance` value clusters occupations with very different cognitive-rhythm signatures — the working musician (performance-peak with long preparation valleys) vs. the freelance writer (sustained solitary concentration) vs. the photographer (visual scanning, high sustained attention in bursts) — and each produces a different relationship with time and attention.

The social-demand axis and its identity implications: O*NET codes occupations by contact-with-others frequency, coordinate-with-others demand, and supervise-others demand. The `service-customer-facing` value clusters bartenders (high social demand, short interaction units, ambient performance) with mortgage brokers (high social demand, long negotiation units, formal-register performance) with the same label, despite their social demand profiles being structurally different.

Body-as-vocational-residue and vocation-past-retirement: OT practitioners who work with retired workers know that vocational demand profiles persist as injury patterns, posture habits, and physical capability into old age. The brief explicitly calls out `§2.9 Embodied practice: vocation produces bodies — gait, hands, posture, signature wear`. The OT demand-profile lens is exactly the right tool to assess whether each proposed value produces a distinct and recognizable embodied residue.

The sedentary/active split within `tech-work` and `commerce-large`: both values cluster almost entirely in the sedentary-light physical demand range, but differ on cognitive-load profile (tech: sustained problem-decomposition; commerce-large: sustained social-negotiation and information-integration). The OT would note that `tech-work` and `commerce-large` produce similarly sedentary bodies but very different attention-rhythm identities — the question is whether the game needs to encode this.

severity_examples.condition: This is a direct conflict with a stated design principle: the vocation value needs to predict body-formation, but `caregiver` spans OT demand profiles that produce incoherent body signatures
severity_examples.scenario: The brief states that `§2.9 Embodied practice: vocation produces bodies — gait, hands, posture, signature wear` and that `different vocations produce different walks`. The `caregiver` value clusters the EMT (high physical demand, musculoskeletal injury pattern, operational-rhythm body) with the K-12 teacher (sedentary-light, sustained-attention demand, institutional-posture body) — two occupations that produce completely different physical residues. When generating embodied characteristics for a `caregiver` Unc, the system cannot know which body to generate.

severity_examples.condition: When generating a `creative-freelance` Unc, the system cannot distinguish the musician's body (instrument-shaped hands, performance posture, night-economy temporal identity) from the writer's body (chair-shaped posture, eye-strain, daytime solitude identity)
severity_examples.scenario: The working musician (OT profile: performance-peak attention rhythm, fine-motor instrumental skill, irregular sleep/work schedule, high physical demand during performance, sedentary during composition) and the working writer (OT profile: sustained solitary concentration, sedentary-light, regular self-scheduled work rhythm) are both `creative-freelance` but have entirely different demand-profile signatures that produce different bodies, different psychological signatures, and different vocation-as-identity structures

severity_examples.condition: The brief wants each vocation to carry metis `the credential system cannot see` — the OT demand-profile records the physical residue of that metis in the body. `land-work` is over-aggregated if it produces indistinguishable bodies.
severity_examples.scenario: O*NET data shows that `land-work` occupations span the full physical-demand range from light (greenhouse worker, poultry farmer with automation) to very heavy (commercial fisher, logger, ranch hand) — but the OT demand-profile for commercial fishing (extreme weather exposure, heavy lifting, boat-movement proprioceptive demands) produces a body-knowledge and proprioceptive identity that distinguishes the commercial fisher from the grain farmer in ways that become visible in posture, hand callus pattern, and gait

spec.source_domain: Occupational therapy, functional capacity evaluation, O*NET Work Activities and Work Context taxonomy, Dictionary of Occupational Titles physical demand ratings
success_hints: The DOT/O*NET physical demand levels (sedentary, light, medium, heavy, very heavy) and the primary exertion type (climbing, reaching, handling, fingering, feeling) are a quick diagnostic for body-coherence within a proposed vocation value — run the 13 values through this test

The OT concept of 'functional capacity' — what a body can still do after decades of a particular demand profile — is the right lens for evaluating `vocation_formative` × `way-depth = lifer` character generation. What does this Unc's body still remember?

Attention rhythm (burst vs. sustained vs. ambient) is as identity-forming as physical demand — the surgeon's burst-peak attention and the long-haul driver's sustained monotonic attention produce different cognitive identities even if both are `professional-credentialed` or `trades-transport` coded

Emotional-labor demand is a real OT measurement category (O*NET codes: Social Perceptiveness, Emotional Intelligence requirements) — the difference between a nurse's emotional-labor demand and an electrician's is vocationally constitutive and should produce different Unc personality-facet distributions downstream
spec.task_context: Reviewing a proposed 13-value vocation-coding axis for Unc Rancher, a procedural-generation system for recognizable older-male character archetypes. spec.decision_lens: Is the chosen sample interval sufficient to detect the smallest shadow feature that materially changes routing weight, and has the error bound been quantified?
spec.distance_rationale: PCI surveyors divide a road network into sample units and choose station intervals to balance labor cost against detection error — exactly the trade-off between 5 m vs 10 m shadow sample spacing.
spec.expected_isomorphisms: The PCI 'sample unit' maps to a GraphML edge; the distress observation at each station maps to a sun/shade pixel read. spec.name: fd-pavement-survey-cadence
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a pavement management engineer who conducts PCI surveys per ASTM D6433, designing station intervals to balance field effort against statistical detection of localized distress.
review_areas: Whether a fixed 5 m interval is justified relative to the spatial autocorrelation of shadow patterns — building overhangs may cast shadows narrower than 5 m, making them systematically invisible
The 'min 2 samples per edge' rule for edges < 5 m — whether endpoint-only sampling on short edges introduces position-dependent bias when an edge straddles a shadow boundary
Absence of any variance or confidence metric on sun_fraction — PCI reports confidence intervals per sample unit; the brainstorm delivers only a point estimate with no uncertainty signal to Phase 1.6
Whether the 5 m interval was chosen empirically (sweep and compare) or assumed — PCI practice requires a sampling adequacy check (typically a pilot survey at 2x density to verify results converge)

The interaction between Shapely interpolate arc-length spacing and raster pixel boundaries — samples may cluster at pixel edges when interval aligns with pixel size multiples, introducing spatial aliasing

The missing sensitivity analysis: at what sample interval does mean sun_fraction change by more than 0.05 on a representative DTLA block? This threshold should be documented before the interval is locked.

severity_examples.example: No variance or standard error is stored per edge. Phase 1.6 has no signal for edges with high within-edge shadow variability (e.g., a 200 m boulevard that is 90% sun but has a 20 m solid-canopy midblock section). The routing weight formula treats a uniform sun_fraction=0.8 identically to a volatile one — a calibration gap that should at minimum be flagged with a data quality annotation.

The 5 m interval is stated but never validated. PCI procedure requires a 'sampling adequacy' check — run at 2.5 m and confirm sun_fraction values stabilize. Without this, the interval is an engineering guess, not a calibrated parameter. The --sample-interval-m flag exists but the brainstorm records no empirical basis for the default.

The --report histogram shows distribution shape but discards within-edge variability. A bimodal edge (half shade, half sun) and a uniform edge with sun_fraction=0.5 look identical in the aggregate. A secondary metric like 'shade run count' or 'max contiguous shade run length' would distinguish them for future calibration.

spec.decision_lens: Where does the brainstorm's formula or its default parameters produce weights that either fail to discriminate routes by shade or produce non-monotonic outcomes relative to pedestrian comfort expectations?
spec.focus: Walking/pedestrian routing formula correctness: felt-minute model validity, sun_coefficient calibration, pace_mps defaults, perceived-cost model assumptions, unit consistency
spec.name: fd-pedestrian-routing-formula
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of a pedestrian routing researcher familiar with thermal comfort and perceived-cost walking models — they care about whether the felt-minute formula produces outputs that meaningfully discriminate route quality in practice, measure validity by whether the formula's outputs for representative DTLA edges produce weights that a routing engine would use to prefer shaded routes, and flag anywhere that default coefficients, unit handling, or formula structure produce degenerate or misleading weights.
review_areas: The formula felt_minutes = (length_m / pace_mps / 60) * (1 + 0.5 * sun_fraction) produces a sun penalty multiplier in [1.0, 1.5] — the maximum penalty for a fully sunny edge is 50% over a fully shaded edge of the same length. The brainstorm notes synthesis finding 65 suggests this may not discriminate in DTLA's regular grid but does not document the implied trade-off: the optimizer accepts up to a 50% longer route for full shade over full sun. This is the primary UX policy statement of the formula and should be explicitly documented.

The formula treats sun_fraction as a linear penalty factor — this is a simplification relative to UTCI (Phase 2), which is nonlinear in solar radiation. The v0 formula makes shade preference independent of absolute walking time: a 1-second sunny edge costs 1.5x a 1-second shaded edge, same as a 10-minute edge. The routing optimizer is equally willing to take a 1-second detour to avoid a 1-second sunny edge as a 10-minute detour to avoid a 10-minute sunny edge — the brainstorm does not document whether this linear scaling is intentional for v0.

The default pace_mps = 1.4 m/s is ~5.0 km/h, consistent with typical adult walking pace. However, the formula uses pace_mps only to convert length_m to walking_minutes — it does not affect the sun penalty multiplier. A pace_mps=1.1 (StepsDaddy stroll mode) produces longer walking_minutes but the same relative sun penalty. The brainstorm notes 'persona-aware pace = different FeltMinutesV0 instance' but does not verify that slower pace does not cause unexpected routing artifacts on very short sunny detours.

The formula assumes length_m is in meters and pace_mps is in m/s, producing walking_minutes in minutes — this is dimensionally correct. However, edge_attrs.get('length', 0.0) trusts the OSMnx-provided length attribute. The brainstorm does not verify that the Phase 1.5 GraphML preserves the length attribute with meter units after projection, or that reprojection from WGS84 changes the stored length value.

The NaN fallback policies assign sf values of 0.5 ('neutral'), nan_fallback_value, 0.0 ('shade'), or 1.0 ('sun'). The 'neutral' policy rationale states 'the router neither preferences nor avoids unknown-coverage edges' — but sf=0.5 produces a 1.25x multiplier, meaning unknown edges cost 25% more than fully shaded. The router does modestly prefer unknown-coverage over sunny (1.25x vs 1.5x) — calling this 'neutral' is inaccurate and could mislead Phase 1.7 calibration.

severity_examples.condition: Phase 1.7's route comparison card will show shade% and felt-minutes deltas. If users see the optimal route taking a 45% longer path to gain 90% shade, sun_coefficient=0.5 is the policy making that trade-off — but it is not documented as a policy choice. Calibration in Phase 1.7 that changes sun_coefficient changes the trade-off, and without documentation the 0.5 default looks like an arbitrary placeholder.
severity_examples.scenario: 50% detour limit not documented as the primary UX policy

severity_examples.condition: For a 5-minute trip with one sunny segment and a 60-minute trip with one sunny segment of the same shade fraction, the routing optimizer is proportionally equally willing to detour. This means the felt-minute model does not capture that users tolerate a short sunny stretch on a long walk more than on a short errand — if this is a known v0 limitation, it should be documented.
severity_examples.scenario: Linear sun penalty produces equal routing preference independent of trip length

severity_examples.condition: Calling the 1.25x multiplier 'neutral' is incorrect if the design intent is that unknown-coverage edges have no routing preference. True neutrality would require the unknown multiplier to equal the population-average multiplier of known edges, which depends on the DTLA distribution of sun_fraction values.
severity_examples.scenario: Neutral fallback policy (0.5) is not neutral — it preferences unknown over sunny

success_hints: Add a formula semantics section documenting the maximum shade-preference detour as a function of sun_coefficient: detour_factor = 1 + sun_coefficient, so the default 0.5 means the optimizer accepts up to 50% longer routes for full shade over full sun.

Document that 'neutral' means 'small penalty for unknown edges, not zero penalty' — either rename to 'moderate' or document why 0.5 is the chosen fallback given DTLA's expected sun_fraction distribution.
Verify that the OSMnx length attribute in the Phase 1.5 output GraphML is in meters by spot-checking a known DTLA street segment against measured distance.

spec.decision_lens: Can Phase 1.7's routing server replace the active EdgeWeight instance at runtime (e.g., switching from default pace to stroll pace for a persona) without reloading the graph from disk, and is the Protocol designed to support a weight factory registry?
spec.distance_rationale: PID tuner engineers design controller-flavor swap mechanisms that replace a running controller (P-only → PID → cascade) without stopping the process, requiring the new controller to be initialized from the current state — the same operational pattern as swapping EdgeWeight implementations in a running routing server without requiring a full graph reload.
spec.expected_isomorphisms: The PID 'bumpless transfer' (new controller inherits integral accumulator from the old one at swap time) maps to the Phase 1.7 concern of whether apply_weight can be called mid-session to update felt_minutes without reloading the graph from disk. The PID 'controller flavor registry' (map from flavor-name string to constructor) maps to a weight factory pattern that Phase 1.7's routing API might expose for persona-tier routing (StepsDaddy stroll mode vs. brisk mode).
spec.focus: Runtime substitution ergonomics — whether FeltMinutesV0 and the apply_weight helper support mid-session weight updates without full graph reload, and whether the Protocol enables a weight registry for persona-tier dispatch
spec.name: fd-pid-tuner-hotswap
spec.persona: Apply the perspective of an industrial process-control engineer who designs PID tuning systems with bumpless controller-flavor transfer, hot-swap registries, and parameter introspection endpoints for live operator dashboards.
review_areas: The brainstorm states that Phase 1.7 can choose between (a) call apply_weight once at load and read felt_minutes per edge during A*, or (b) call weight callable lazily per-edge during A*. Option (a) bakes the weight into the graph; option (b) keeps the weight hot-swappable. PID practice: the brainstorm should commit to (b) as the canonical path for live-serving, with (a) as an optimization only for batch/offline use. The current text leaves both equally valid, which will create a split implementation.

The persona-aware pace case (StepsDaddy stroll mode = FeltMinutesV0(pace_mps=1.1)) is mentioned as a different instance, not a schema change. PID hot-swap practice: the routing server needs a weight registry or factory that maps persona-ID to an EdgeWeight instance, and the Protocol should support a display_name or identifier for logging. Without this, persona dispatch is an undocumented caller convention.

apply_weight mutates the graph in place (writes to edge dicts). If option (a) is used and a user switches persona mid-session, apply_weight must be re-called over all 12,880 edges. PID bumpless transfer avoids full-state recomputation; the lazy option (b) avoids the re-run cost entirely but requires A* to call the weight callable per edge rather than reading a pre-computed attribute. The choice has a direct latency impact on persona-switch responsiveness.

The NanFallback Literal type has four values, but there is no mechanism for an operator to inspect which policy is active on the running routing server. PID tuners expose parameter introspection endpoints (current Kp, Ki, Kd, flavor). Phase 1.7's API should expose the active weight instance's repr() or a structured parameter dump so that operator dashboards can display 'routing mode: stroll, sun_coefficient: 0.5, fallback: neutral.'

The Protocol has no version field, which means a weight registry keyed on formula class name alone cannot distinguish FeltMinutesV0 v1 (initial) from FeltMinutesV0 v2 (after Phase 1.7 calibration updates the default coefficient). PID flavor registries version their flavors; the Protocol should carry a version string for registry safety.

The frozen dataclass supports dataclasses.replace() for creating variants, but the brainstorm does not specify a canonical factory pattern for persona-tier instantiation. PID systems use a controller factory that takes persona config and returns a ready-to-run instance; without this, each caller invents its own FeltMinutesV0() initialization convention, leading to config drift across the routing server, the test suite, and any future CLI tools.

The brainstorm should specify which option is canonical for the serving path and which is for offline use, before Phase 1.7 picks one ad hoc.
